deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a Gauss manuscript in the sense of original derivations. It is a printed page (roman numeral xiv, Fraktur type) from the historical introduction of an 18th-century German arithmetic and algebra textbook. The bundle name 'HB.Leiste' points to Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, c. 1790), probably Gauss's own copy. The page contains no calculations, derivations or handwritten annotations. Its content is a narrative history of 17th-century arithmetic and algebra:

(a) Napier's logarithms were spread at once by Ursinus.
(b) Henry Briggs, professor of geometry at Oxford, worked out the more convenient common (base-10) logarithm system, with application to sines and tangents. It displaced Napier's system.
(c) Gellibrand and Adriaan Vlacq of Gouda helped complete the Briggsian tables, which are 'still used'. The text says they first appeared in 1633.
(d) William Brouncker (1620-1684) used a 'series of fractions' to compute the circle, referring to the book's Zusatz to §80. This is his continued fraction for 4/pi.

In algebra:
1) Albert Girard, 'Invention nouvelle en l'algèbre' (1629), first treated the negative and positive roots of a cubic.
2) Thomas Harriot (1560-1621), in 'Artis analyticae praxis' (1631), factored every equation set equal to zero into linear factors (x - r_i) (book §189). He also introduced lowercase letters and juxtaposition for multiplication (Anmerk. §13).
3) Descartes (1596-1650) introduced superscript exponent notation (§40). He admitted negative ('false') roots, gave the rule of signs (§190), and used the method of undetermined coefficients.
4) Wallis (1616-1703) had a prodigious memory and extracted square roots mentally in the dark to 12, even 40, digits; the sentence continues onto the next page (Pelshover).

The page cross-references the textbook's own sections (§80, §189, §13, §40, §190). Nothing mathematical is derived here.
errors: Girard is called 'ein holländischer Mathematiker'; he was born in Lorraine (St-Mihiel) and worked in the Netherlands. This is a minor inaccuracy typical of the period.

Vlacq's 'Arithmetica logarithmica' appeared in 1628. 1633 is the date of Vlacq's 'Trigonometria artificialis' and of the Briggs/Gellibrand 'Trigonometria Britannica'. So '1633' is only partly right for 'the Briggsian tables'.
Harriot's 'Artis analyticae praxis' is posthumous (1631). The text gives no date, so this is not an error, only an omission.
Brouncker's construction is a continued fraction, not a series. 'Reihe von Brüchen' is loose period terminology.
The Wallis mental-arithmetic anecdote is usually reported as extracting the square root of a 53-digit number to 27 places. The '12, even 40 digits' figures are the textbook's version.

results.usually_credited_to: William Brouncker, c. 1655 (published in Wallis's Arithmetica infinitorum, 1656)

results.what: Harriot's factorization of a polynomial equation into linear factors
results.modern_name: Factor theorem / product representation of a polynomial by its roots

results.usually_credited_to: Henry Briggs (1617/1624), Adriaan Vlacq (1628), Henry Gellibrand (1633)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed textbook page (Leiste's Arithmetik und Algebra) giving a standard 18th-century history of 17th-century mathematics. There is no handwriting by Gauss and no derivation, so there is nothing to attribute to him.

checkable.asserts: A truncation of Brouncker's continued fraction 4/pi = 1 + 1^2/(2 + 3^2/(2 + 5^2/(2 + ...))) approximates 4/pi; the difference is small and shrinks slowly with depth.
Harriot-style factorization of a cubic set to zero: the coefficients are elementary symmetric functions of the roots. The result should be 0.
The coefficients [1, 0, -7, 6] have 2 sign changes, matching the 2 positive roots. Substituting -x gives [-1, 0, 7, 6] with 1 change, matching the 1 negative root (Descartes' rule of signs).

transcription_corrections: The page is printed (Fraktur), not handwritten. The machine transcription is essentially accurate.
'resoluendas' reflects the printed long-s/u ligature spelling of 'resolvendas'.
The right edge of the image shows the beginning of the facing page xv ("aus Königsberg..."), which is cut off; it is not part of folio xiv.
